prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Rioting has flared near Belfast on Saturday after the arrests of three men in the killings of two soldiers in Northern Ireland last week, police said. Two people in masks prepare to throw petrol bombs Saturday in Lurgan, Northern Ireland. Petrol bombs have been hurled at police in Lurgan, a town in County Armagh, 20 miles west of Belfast, police in Northern Ireland said. There are gangs of youths on the streets, authorities said, but there have been no arrests or injuries. Police announced the arrests on Saturday and said the three men have been taken to the police service's Serious Crime Suite in County Antrim. One of them, a dissident republican named Colin Duffy, is from Lurgan. They are the first arrests in connection with the March 7 shootings, which were the first fatal attack on British troops in the province for more than 12 years. The two British soldiers were shot dead at a base in Massereene, in Antrim, as they were preparing to ship out for duty in Afghanistan. The soldiers, Cengiz "Pat" Azimkar, 21, and Mark Quinsey, 23, had already packed their bags and changed into desert uniforms, authorities said. Two masked gunmen with automatic rifles shot them as the soldiers picked up a pizza delivery at the barracks, authorities said. Two other soldiers and the two pizza delivery men were seriously wounded. The shooting has sparked fears of a return to the sectarian violence that Northern Ireland suffered until the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, a period known as The Troubles. A militant splinter group, the Real IRA, reportedly claimed it had carried out the attack on the soldiers. Two days after the soldiers were killed, a police officer was killed in a shooting southwest of Belfast. Constable Stephen Carroll was one of four officers who were responding to call in Craigavon when his vehicle came under fire and he was killed. Three people have been arrested in connection with the police officer's death. The Continuity IRA, a republican splinter group that does not accept the Good Friday Agreement, said it had killed Carroll, Britain's Press Association reported. Politicians from across the political spectrum have condemned the killings, with Sinn Fein deputy leader Martin McGuinness calling the killers "traitors to the island of Ireland." Sinn Fein is a predominantly Catholic party that wants Northern Ireland to leave the United Kingdom and become part of the Republic of Ireland. The party is widely thought to be linked to the Irish Republican Army. Danny Kennedy, deputy leader of the loyalist Ulster Unionist Party, which wants Northern Ireland to remain part of the United Kingdom, also condemned the attack as "wicked and murderous."

counterfactuals.output:
**Riots erupt near Belfast after arrests in soldiers’ killings**

**BELFAST, Northern Ireland (CNN)** — Rioters hurled gasoline bombs and other missiles at police near Belfast following the arrests of three men suspected in the March 7 killings of two British soldiers, authorities said.

The unrest broke out in the predominantly nationalist town of Lurgan, southwest of Belfast, where vehicles were hijacked and set on fire and roads were blocked. Police urged residents to avoid the area as officers moved to restore order.

The violence followed the arrests of three men in connection with the shooting deaths of Sappers Mark Quinsey, 23, and Patrick Azimkar, 21, outside Massereene army barracks in Antrim.

The soldiers were collecting pizzas at the entrance to the base when gunmen opened fire. Two other soldiers and two pizza delivery workers were wounded. The dissident republican group known as the Real IRA claimed responsibility.

Northern Ireland’s political leaders condemned both the killings and the subsequent street violence, appealing for calm and warning that dissident groups were trying to undermine the region’s peace process.

The soldiers’ deaths were followed two days later by the fatal shooting of police Constable Stephen Carroll in Craigavon. Another dissident group, the Continuity IRA, claimed responsibility for that attack.

The killings were the first involving British security forces in Northern Ireland in more than a decade and raised fears of renewed sectarian violence despite broad public and political support for the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement.

counterfactuals.output:
- **Lurgan unrest:** Dissident republican tensions led to rioting in Lurgan and nearby Craigavon, with masked youths throwing stones and petrol bombs at police and disrupting roads and rail services. The violence reflected opposition to the peace process and the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI).

- **Massereene Barracks attack, 7 March 2009:** Gunmen opened fire outside Massereene Barracks in Antrim as soldiers collected a pizza delivery. Sappers **Mark Quinsey** and **Patrick Azimkar** were killed; two other soldiers and two delivery workers were wounded. The dissident republican **Real IRA** claimed responsibility.

- **Killing of Constable Stephen Carroll, 9 March 2009:** Two days later, PSNI Constable **Stephen Carroll** was shot dead in Craigavon while responding to a report apparently designed to lure police into an ambush. The **Continuity IRA**, another dissident republican organization, claimed responsibility.

Both killings were widely condemned by Northern Ireland’s political parties and were viewed as attempts by dissident republicans to destabilize the peace process.

# Petrol bombs thrown at police after arrest of dissident republican Colin Duffy and two men

**LURGAN, Northern Ireland —** Police officers have come under petrol-bomb attack in Lurgan following the arrest of prominent dissident republican Colin Duffy and two other men in a terrorism investigation.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said officers and police vehicles were targeted during disorder in the County Armagh town after news of the arrests emerged. Petrol bombs and other missiles were thrown, prompting police to warn residents to avoid the affected area while security operations continued.

No serious injuries were immediately reported. Police were assessing damage to their vehicles and maintaining a presence in the area amid concern that the unrest could continue.

Duffy, a long-standing figure in dissident republicanism, was detained alongside two other men by detectives investigating suspected terrorist activity. The men were being questioned under terrorism legislation. Police had not disclosed full details of the suspected offences or identified the other detainees at the time of the initial announcement.

The arrests and subsequent violence come amid continuing concern over groups opposed to the Northern Ireland peace process. Dissident republican organisations reject the 1998 Good Friday Agreement and remain committed to using violence in pursuit of a united Ireland, although they command little public support.

The PSNI condemned the attack, saying petrol bombs pose an indiscriminate threat not only to officers but also to residents, motorists and children. Such devices can cause fatal burns and rapidly ignite vehicles or nearby homes.

Police appealed for calm and urged community representatives to use their influence to prevent further disorder. They also asked anyone with video footage or information about those involved in the attacks to contact investigators.

Political representatives were expected to condemn the violence and call for those responsible to be brought before the courts. Attacks on police remain a particularly sensitive issue in Northern Ireland, where officers continue to face a severe threat from dissident republican organisations despite the broad decline in paramilitary violence since the peace agreement.

Security operations were continuing, and roads in the affected part of Lurgan could remain restricted while police examined the scene and gathered evidence. Authorities said further updates would be issued as the investigation developed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the recent violence in Northern Ireland, including the deaths of soldiers Cengiz “Pat” Azimkar and Mark Quinsey, fears of a return to The Troubles, and political reactions to the killings.
counterfactuals.output:
In March 2009, Northern Ireland suffered its most serious burst of dissident republican violence since the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.

- **7 March — Massereene Barracks:** Gunmen opened fire outside the British Army base in Antrim as soldiers collected pizzas shortly before deploying to Afghanistan. Sappers **Cengiz “Pat” Azimkar**, 21, and **Mark Quinsey**, 23, were killed. Four other people, including two pizza delivery workers, were wounded. The **Real IRA**, a breakaway republican group opposed to the peace settlement, claimed responsibility.
- **9 March — Craigavon:** Two days later, Police Service of Northern Ireland officer **Stephen Carroll** was shot dead while responding to a call. The **Continuity IRA**, another dissident faction, claimed that killing.

The attacks prompted fears of a return to **the Troubles**, the decades-long conflict involving republican and loyalist paramilitaries and British security forces. Dissident groups appeared to be trying to undermine the power-sharing government, provoke a heavy security response, and revive sectarian confrontation.

However, political leaders stressed that the circumstances were very different from those of the Troubles. The dissidents had little public support, the main republican movement had accepted constitutional politics, and both nationalist and unionist leaders remained committed to power-sharing. Security was tightened and arrests followed, but officials resisted treating the attacks as evidence that the peace process was collapsing.

The political reaction was unusually united:

- British Prime Minister **Gordon Brown** and Irish Taoiseach **Brian Cowen** condemned the killings and pledged cooperation.
- Northern Ireland First Minister **Peter Robinson** and Deputy First Minister **Martin McGuinness** appeared together to defend the political settlement.
- McGuinness, a former senior IRA figure, denounced those responsible as **“traitors to the island of Ireland,”** a particularly significant rejection of dissident violence.
- Sinn Féin, the DUP, other Northern Irish parties, and community leaders urged the public not to be drawn into retaliation or sectarian disorder.

Thus, while the killings were a severe shock and demonstrated that dissident republican groups remained capable of lethal attacks, the broad political and public response suggested that they did not have the support needed to restart the Troubles on their former scale.

**BELFAST, Northern Ireland —** Police were assessing security across Northern Ireland after rioting near Belfast on Saturday and separate attacks claimed by the dissident republican Real IRA and Continuity IRA.

The unrest involved youths throwing missiles at police and damaging property. Police moved into the area to restore order and appealed for witnesses and information about those responsible.

The violence came amid renewed activity by dissident groups opposed to Northern Ireland’s peace settlement. The Real IRA and Continuity IRA, both breakaway factions of the Irish Republican Army, have rejected the 1998 Good Friday Agreement and continued sporadic attacks despite lacking broad public support.

Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness, a former senior IRA figure, condemned the violence and said those responsible had no mandate and were acting against the interests of the community.

Danny Kennedy of the Ulster Unionist Party also denounced the attacks, describing them as futile and urging the public to cooperate with police.

Authorities said the incidents would not derail Northern Ireland’s political process. Police continued investigations and maintained an increased presence in affected areas.
